article.title: National Anthem
article.author: Chuck Yates
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Several weeks ago, our college football team upset a higher-ranked opponent to remain undefeated. There was a lot of fist bumping among the fans as we all went home feeling vindicated for our faith in the team and the coaches. Before the game, as always, there was the National Anthem. We all stood, removed our hats, and placed our right hands over our hearts in reverent silence, honoring the flag, our liberty, and the military, celebrating “the land of the free and the home of the brave.” The ritual of the flag and the National Anthem links American pride with American wars, American freedom with American violence, American athletes with American troops. And when the Anthem ends, the fans all cheer. It’s tradition, after all—the standing, the bare heads, the hands on hearts, the silent, reverent focus, even the cheers. We do it because we’ve always done it, we say. That’s how traditions work. That’s what makes them traditions. Only we haven’t always done it. It’s an invented tradition—“a set of practices, normally governed by overtly or tacitly accepted rules and of a ritual or symbolic nature, which seek to inculcate certain values and norms of behaviour by repetition,” as British historian Eric Hobsbawn puts it. The repetition, he says, “automatically implies continuity with the past.” Related: Major Jason Watson, Trump, and the Military’s Duty to Defy Illegal Orders As the story goes, our flag ritual originated in the first game of the 1918 World Series, between the Boston Red Sox and the Chicago Cubs. During the seventh inning stretch the band played “The Star Spangled Banner”—which was not the National Anthem until 1931. Fans were already on their feet, and when a player on leave from the military turned toward the flag and saluted, the other players on the field removed their hats and placed their hands over hearts. The fans followed suit, and we’ve been doing it ever since. By now, that spontaneous demonstration of 1918 has acquired an aura of the sacred and eternal. And those who hold it sacred have no tolerance for dissent, as athletes like John Carlos, Tommy Smith, Colin Kaepernick, and others have learned. Outside the rodeo ground next to the football stadium are signs that read: “You are now entering rodeo grounds. You will encounter American flags, the National Anthem, prayer, & dirt flying. If this offends you, please turn around and head home.” In other words, if you don’t like our rituals, we don’t want you here. This is Aaron Tippin singing “I pledge allegiance to this flag, and if that bothers you, well, that's too bad.” It’s Merle Haggard singing “If you don’t love it, leave it.” It echoes the sentiment of a tee shirt I sometimes see a fan wearing. It has an image of the flag with a caption that reads, “If this flag offends you, I’ll help you pack.” This is patriotism understood not as love of country but as open hostility toward anyone who seems to question or criticize either the ritual or the sentiment associated with it. And because fans hear only the first stanza of Francis Scott Key’s poem, they may not know that, like the ritual it legitimizes, it also links freedom and national pride with religious faith and military violence, and has no kind words for dissenters. In its third stanza it boasts: “And where is that band who so vauntingly swore, That the havoc of war and the battle's confusion, A home and a Country should leave us no more? Their blood has wash'd out their foul footstep's pollution. No refuge could save the hireling and slave, From the terror of flight, or the gloom of the grave, And the star-spangled banner in triumph doth wave, O'er the land of the free and the home of the brave." No tolerance for dissent here. Disrespect the flag, or the republic for which it stands, and it’s “When you're runnin’ down our country, hoss, you're walkin’ on the fightin’ side of me.” Related: Things We Have Lost And the fourth stanza proclaims: “O! thus be it ever, when freemen shall stand between their lov’d home and the war’s desolation. Blest with victory and peace, may the Heaven rescued land praise the power that hath made and preserved us a nation! Then conquer we must, when our cause it is just. And this be our motto: ‘in God is our trust.’” Threaten our liberty, our homes, our way of life, and, with God on our side, “we’ll put a boot in your ass, it’s the American way.” There’s certainly nothing wrong with patriotism, or with the flag and the National Anthem. But we need to disconnect them from our exorbitant pride in our military power, our overweening amoral righteousness, our intolerance of dissent, our hostility toward those who don’t look like us, or live like us. Otherwise, “conquer we must” will always be our motto, and we’ll continue to wage unprovoked war on people who’ve posed no threat to us, done us no harm, issued no challenge—always telling ourselves that our cause is just.
